new_en: (36) "He should not perform the brit milah." We are concerned that, because he has never performed it before, he may make a mistake and thereby desecrate Shabbos where no mitzvah was accomplished. The same applies if he has never performed priyah: he may not perform priyah for the first time on Shabbos. A mohel who states that he has already performed a brit milah once on a weekday is believed and need not bring proof. Rama at the end of Yoreh De'ah, siman 266, writes that ideally it is proper to be stringent not to divide 1 Shabbos brit milah between 2 mohalim, 1 cutting and the other performing priyah; rather, the one who cuts should also perform priyah. Many later authorities permit dividing the procedure, and this is the established custom in Poland both on weekdays and on Shabbos. Chayei Adam writes that one should at least not divide the procedure among 3 people, and that the person performing priyah should also perform metzitzah. Yeshuot Yaakov rejects this and permits metzitzah to be performed by another person because it is a separate matter. (37) "On Shabbos." Regarding Yom Tov, one may certainly be lenient on the second day of Yom Tov in the Diaspora. Concerning the first day there is a dispute among the later authorities. If he knows that he is capable of performing the brit milah and there is no other mohel, there is certainly no reason to be stringent. (38) "He may perform the brit milah on Shabbos." This is so even if another mohel is present who has already performed many procedures. (39) "Even," etc. This excludes the view that a father should not personally perform his son's brit milah on Shabbos when another mohel is available, on the ground that for the father it is a psik reisha that is beneficial to him because he is thereby completing the repair of his son. We do not say this. The same beneficial consequence exists for another mohel as well, since he comes specifically to perform the mitzvah, yet the Torah permitted the act. [Terumat HaDeshen]

Seif 10. Regarding a person who has never performed a brit milah, I am uncertain whether the same law applies on Yom Tov, or whether it is permitted on Yom Tov. The source of the restriction is derived from the sugya in Beitzah concerning an act that requires examination. At first glance, since in siman 498, seif 8, we rule leniently regarding the unresolved question of a bird that was trampled, and therefore the concern in heating new tiles is that they may crack, Mordechai's proof would not stand. One can answer that the reason we rule leniently there is necessarily that on Yom Tov the act is permitted by Torah law under the principle of mitoch, leaving only a rabbinic doubt. Accordingly, regarding brit milah on Shabbos we are stringent because the unresolved question concerns a Torah-level doubt. If so, on Yom Tov, where wounding for a Yom Tov need is permitted, there is room to permit the brit milah and to resolve the uncertainty leniently, understanding the concern in heating tiles as one of cracking. Moreover, Tosafos, Megillah 4a, s.v. Veya'avirenah, write that a person does not perform a brit milah unless he is skilled, which implies that this is simply not the ordinary practice, not that there is an independent prohibition. Ran in the first chapter likewise labors to explain why we do not decree concerning a Shabbos brit milah lest one go to an expert, which appears to indicate that he does not accept Mordechai's ruling as practical halacha. Therefore there is room to rely on this on Yom Tov, where the Shulchan Aruch does not state an explicit prohibition.

In Taz, seif katan 2: "a time for tefillin," even rabbinically. According to the view that Shabbos is a time for tefillin, only 1 pair may be brought in, because wearing an additional pair is prohibited because of Bal Tosif. According to the view that Shabbos is not a time for tefillin, 2 pairs may be brought in, because there is no Bal Tosif here even rabbinically. This is Taz's intent, although a few words are missing from the text. It cannot be explained that the underlying distinction is whether violation of Bal Tosif requires intent, or anything similar, because the Gemara implies that the first Tanna's reason is that he violates Bal Tosif even without intent, and that is not actually so. Moreover, if that were the point, what would be the reasoning of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel? Even if intent were required, the extra pair should still be considered a burden. If one were to say that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rejects that consideration, then their dispute would not concern whether intent is required for Bal Tosif, but whether the additional pair is considered a burden. Rather, they dispute Bal Tosif alone: according to the first Tanna, one violates Bal Tosif here even without intent. In this setting, however, the Bal Tosif concern is only rabbinic. Taz therefore had to explain that the other proposed answers do not stand.

[11] [Levush] "But," etc. The wording of the Shulchan Aruch is missing here: one must be careful not to write with liquid on a table or in ashes, but, etc. If one writes with a finger in honey or in congealed fat in the same manner as one writes in ashes, it is forbidden. [Perishah] I found in the Tosefta, chapter 12: if one writes with nutshells, pomegranate peels, congealed blood, congealed milk, on an olive leaf, carob leaf, gourd leaf, or upon any enduring material, he is liable. If he writes upon a lettuce leaf, leek leaf, onion leaf, vegetable leaf, or upon any non-enduring material, he is exempt. The rule is this: if he writes with an enduring substance upon a non-enduring surface, or with a non-enduring substance upon an enduring surface, he is exempt; he is liable only when he writes with an enduring substance upon an enduring surface. This teaches that both the substance used for the writing and the surface upon which it is written must endure for Torah liability. Writing in dust, ashes, liquids, or similar temporary substances is therefore not Torah-level writing, though it remains forbidden rabbinically. Likewise, forming recognizable letters with a finger in a substance that retains their form temporarily is forbidden even though the writing will not endure permanently. The laws of erasing follow the same basic distinction: Torah liability requires erasing in a manner connected with enduring writing, while temporary erasure can nevertheless be rabbinically forbidden. Accordingly, one must be careful with letters formed on foods, wax, or other materials when breaking, smoothing, or manipulating them would intentionally create or erase recognizable writing.
